#6696. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6692. How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Wrapping Gifts

I am one of the messiest people I know, and I come by that reputation honestly. Legend has it that when my parents first met at a party at my mom’s apartment, my dad walked up to her to say that she should probably call the police; he’d passed her bedroom while in search of the bathroom and seen the window wrenched open, with belongings strewn all over the floor. He suggested that she report a robbery—but no, she was forced to admit; that was just how she lived.

I’ve inherited her struggles with neatness and attention to detail. While other mother-daughter duos brought in perfectly stenciled posters and Balthazar-quality brownies to class presentations and bake sales, our attempts were somewhat more haphazard, typically following screaming fights in the aisles of the Staples on 81st and Broadway about what qualified as “nice” graph paper.

When it comes to Christmas, my mom and I have always been aligned on caring more about gathering the people we love to drink mulled wine and watch A Diva’s Christmas Carol for the hundredth time than creating some holiday tableau fit for Instagram. Yet this holiday season finds me in a new place in my life. Since going through a major breakup last year, I’ve tackled all kinds of things that I didn’t previously know I could do, from fixing my hyperactive car battery without a man’s paid-for help to retiling my very own bathroom floor. Was it possible that I could also become the kind of person who looked forward to—or at least didn’t totally dread—my very least favorite Christmas chore, wrapping presents?

I love shopping, I love seeing someone open what I’ve bought for them, and when I was a kid, I loved carrying already-wrapped gifts down the stairs and arranging them under the tree. But there’s something about the finicky, frilly act of wrapping and taping and bow-tying that makes me revert to that chaotic middle-schooler with the slapped-together bake sale contribution; I hate it, but I also hate hating it.

So, a few weeks ago, I decided to break the cycle. I contacted It’s A Wrap, a gift-wrapping studio and floral boutique in Studio City, Los Angeles, to ask one simple question: Could a Christmas flop like me really be taught to make a gift look great?

Y Lane, who co-owns It’s A Wrap with partner Carolyn Haywood, has seen it all when it comes to outlandishly LA-coded gifting requests. (Ask her about the time she gift-wrapped a flat-screen TV for a guy’s Playboy Bunny girlfriend on Christmas Day.) But her patience as she walked me through the basics of wrapping—assembling a box; figuring out how much tape to use; creating clean, crease-free corners—was still amazing, given that I’ve had not one but two driving instructors quit on me and, for all I know, made any number of math and science tutors seek workers’ compensation.

I’m far from Y Lane’s first student; she offers gift-wrapping lessons semi-regularly at It’s A Wrap’s cozy, Santa’s-workshop-reminiscent storefront off Tujunga Avenue (that is, if Santa’s workshop were regularly passed by shirtless bros and Alo-clad beach babes sipping iced lattes from Aroma down the street). Demand predictably increases during the holiday season, which, for her, starts well before Halloween and stretches until the beginning of January.

I got the parts with the box and the paper pretty quickly, but once we got into the specifics of bow-tying, my mind went blank. I couldn’t tie a bow in my ponytail for school spirit day or French-braid the other girls’ hair at camp to save my life, so why would I be able to now?

Slowly but surely, though, my efforts came together into a sort-of bow, which Y Lane complimented and then promptly untied, instructing me to try a few more. “The nicer the box is, the easier it is to wrap,” Y Lane told me. “The most important word in wrapping is measure.”

A few weeks later, I have a stack of neatly wrapped gifts piled up under my little pink tree impressively early. And who’s to say? Maybe I’ll also become the person who saves the wrapping paper for next year.

There are very few beauty products that unite the entire ELLE beauty team. There is one recent launch, however, that we are all obsessed with, and we’re not the only ones. When Victoria Beckham Beauty’s The Foundation Drops launched last year, they were met first with curiosity (this is a foundation that costs $110, after all), and then adoration, as we all discovered that actually, yes, this little 30ml bottle is indeed worth its weight in gold. In fact, we loved these tinted drops so much that we wrote a dedicated review of them.

Victoria Beckham was never going to release a subpar complexion product, but this silky foundation is truly beyond expectations. The viral bestseller works beautifully on all skin types and textures, skimming over enlarged pores, thread veins, and acne scars with ease, and bringing luminous life back to more mature complexions too.

The secret is all in the texture. As a serum foundation, it feels more like an oil than a viscous liquid and skims over the skin to leave behind a glowing (never greasy) veil of coverage. The coverage is light-medium and completely buildable, so you likely won’t need to team it with a concealer. Beckham called on German medical scientist and skin care kingpin Augustinus Bader to help create the formula, which is infused with his signature TFC8 blend of minerals and vitamins. So in short, your skin will look better with and without the foundation on.

Why am I telling you all this? Well, if you were one of the many who snorted at the idea of a triple-figure foundation, today is your day: For Black Friday, Victoria Beckham Beauty is having a site-wide sale, including a 20 percent reduction on the only foundation you’ll ever want to use again. Our advice? Stock up and buy two: there is absolutely no chance you won’t love it.

In fact, this isn't the only VBB product deserving of a spot in your kit. Ahead of party season, the Satin Kajal Liner is the obvious winner: creamy, blendable, and available in a growing number of jewel tones, it's little wonder this note-perfect eye pencil is Beckham's bestselling product. Similarly, the Longwear Eyeshadow Sticks are excellent for festive nights. If you, like me, find shadows and palettes too much of a faff, they're bound to please: simply scribble over your lid and blend the edges for a perfect smoky eye.

Okay, one last recommendation before you go forth and shop: Victoria Beckham's fragrances are in a league of their own. Suite 302 is the one to gift yourself for Christmas: with tart cherry atop a lingering trail of tobacco and leather, it's perfectly wintry and incredibly sexy.

#6686. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6685. Solawave’s Black Friday BOGO Deal Lets You Gift an LED Mask—and Keep One

Save up to $400 on celebrity-loved, expert-vetted red light therapy devices.

Red light therapy devices are one of the best gifts you can give a skin care lover. Luckily, we spotted this Black Friday deal from Solawave that’s too good to skip, especially at the peak of the holiday shopping rush. The editor-approved brand is running a buy-one-get-one-free promotion through December 31, meaning you can gift a red light therapy device to someone you love and get one for yourself at no extra cost.

Solawave’s viral skin care wand is included in the BOGO promotion, but our beauty editors agree it’s worth investing in the brand’s red light therapy mask, so you can treat your entire face at once, hands-free. According to double board-certified plastic surgeon Amir Karam, M.D., red light therapy devices such as this “can increase collagen production to ward off fine lines and wrinkles, improve skin texture and tone, reduce inflammation, and boost blood circulation, which can create a more youthful complexion.”

The FDA-cleared mask features a flexible design with more than 300 LED lights for total coverage. Those seeking targeted treatments could try Solawave’s Eye Recovery Pro and Neck & Chest Pro Mask, which rank among our experts’ top light therapy devices for eyes and neck, respectively.

Solawave devices utilize deep red light, amber light, and near-infrared technology to reach different depths of the skin. As a result, they’re more effective at promoting collagen and elastin production, reducing inflammation, and calming redness than devices that rely on a single wavelength. Treatments take less than 5 minutes, and with consistent use, you can expect to see results within a few weeks to months.

Used by celebrities such as Nicole Kidman, Reese Witherspoon, and Sabrina Carpenter, Solawave’s 4-in-1 Skincare Wand is a lower-commitment gift. Pooja Rambhia, M.D., a board-certified dermatologist at UnionDerm in New York City, explains that the handheld wand “combines red light therapy with microcurrent, therapeutic warmth, and facial massage, making it a multifunctional tool for stimulating collagen, improving skin tone, and enhancing product absorption.”

Solawave’s palm-sized 2-in-1 Skincare Mini device works particularly well for hand and body treatments; it uses red and near-infrared light to improve skin firmness and elasticity, and warms to help soothe and depuff. Plus, the compact design makes it easy to pack for travel or sneak in sessions on the go.

Solawave’s BOGO sale runs through the end of the year, but products could sell out before then. The best part of all? You can use the device you get for yourself right away.

#6684. Black Friday 2026 Is a Good Time to Buy a Great Suit

Black Friday is back with a vengeance, here to take revenge on all the times you were made to pay full price this year. And while many men decide to focus only on ordering discounted casual clothes and tech deals, here’s an even better idea: Turn this into the historic day that you finally become the owner of a suit you actually love.

Not the one you bought in a rush for that wedding this summer, or the hand-me-down that fits badly, but not badly enough to get rid of. No, it’s time to say enough is enough: I am an adult, and I will own at least one suit that makes me look incredible, and feel even better than that.

And there really is no better time. Because while a discount on face wash might save you might save you four dollars, a 50% markdown on a suit—and yes, those currently exist—can save you hundreds, if not thousands of them. And of course, you’re not just getting a suit here, you’re also getting two separates: The jacket also goes with jeans, the dress pants also go with tees.

And remember, there’s no need to worry too much about figuring out a perfect fit over the internet: Put a fraction of the savings you’re making towards a trip to the tailor once it arrives, and the suit will look (and feel) like it was made for only you by the end of the week. Below, all of today’s deals that truly stand out from the rest.

Want more savings intel? Start with our guide to the best Cyber Monday clothing deals, then make moves to GQ's all-in-one master list of every Cyber Week deal that matters.

Banana Republic is taking as much as 50% off of its greatest hits this Black Friday. We've got a full edit of the sale rack here, but when it comes to suiting, the first set that caught my eye was this classic, sharp navy guy. I think it's because after years of wider fits and earthy tones, there's now something sharp and animating about a classic, fitted, formal-leaning suit. And if your office still calls for one, this deal looks even better.

It would be wrong to call Barena up-and-coming—its roots go back more than half a century, after all. But I can tell you that it's growing in renown, and incredible pieces like this virgin wool suit offered at a surprisingly fair price even before the discount are exactly why.

Sid Mashburn's best suits—including this one—are fully canvassed to mould more to your frame with every wear, creating a damn near bespoke fit over time. And today only, a true stunner from the line is 25% off.

This might be the most unexpected, handsome jacket on this list. Yes, it's more summer-coded, but with that shade of brown and lapels that gentle, you could just as easily wear it to a nice dinner on a Thursday night over a toasty turtleneck.

In case you hadn’t noticed, we’re huge fans of the double-breasted suit these days. Here’s a classic of the form from Canali that you can save literally over $1,000 on today. Yes, it’s still an investment, but you’re getting peak lapels, padded shoulders, a full lining, a 100% wool outer, and a 100% cupro lining. Which is sort of unheard of at this price point.

This Black Friday is so legit, even Saman Amel—yes, the Stockholm label that everybody loves but almost nobody can afford—is 40% off, and therefore 40% more possible. (One day, I will meet Mr Porter himself, and I will kneel to thank him.)

The man behind Paul Smith didn't become Sir Paul Smith for nothing. Instead, he was recognized for decades of making men look and feel handsome in sharp, made-in-Italy suits with hidden details (a colorful lining here, a fun buttonhole stitch there) that are as charming and uplifting as the man himself. Know, too, that he's one of the few independent owners left of his generation: Every sale goes right back to the man himself.

If you can see yourself wearing your suits with T-shirts and sweaters as much as fine shirting, then a more relaxed suit from Second Layer might be the one for you. Those pants are an especially great option for wearing as separates, too.

When New York's coolest custom tailor, Jake Mueser, permitted Mr Porter to sell his ready-to-wear creations this year, cheers rang out around GQ towers. The Waverly cut is the house speciality–svelte, but not severe.

It also comes in this incredible double-breasted 6x2 with peak lapels, and matching high-rise trousers. Normally it's only discounted in linen this time of year, but right now it's available for less in exquisite virgin wool.

As we've said before, Mfpen produces Scandinavian minimalism that's actually fun to wear. (Its most recent office-wear collection, for example, was inspired by “what would happen if mall goths were forced to get corporate jobs.”) That cool factor is great, but what really sets the brand apart is its use of quality deadstock materials, keeping prices down and the planet happy. Reward them with your dollar, and look five times more handsome for it.

Not all suits need to scream leading man. Some can—and should—communicate that you're a wise, thoughtful, dependable fellow who has stories to tell and places to be. Todd Snyder's Madison suit, in a neppy Italian silk-Donegal wool blend, is exactly that number.

The Todd Snyder savings continue with this discount on the relaxed Wythe suit, which takes a cut that would work in literally any setting, and improves it further with the panache of Italian cashmere.

#6681. Cameron Diaz in ‘The Holiday’ Is My Winter Style Inspiration

Have you seen Nancy Meyers’s The Holiday recently? If not, now is the best time to rewatch the 2006 classic rom-com, as it officially turns 20 next month—and will even be returning to theaters for a limited run.

If you’ve never witnessed the genius film, it stars Cameron Diaz and Kate Winslet as two single women who do a house swap over the holidays. Hollywood editor Amanda (Diaz) relocates to the English countryside, while journalist Iris (Winslet) touches down in Los Angeles. Both end up meeting men—Jude Law and Jack Black, no less—and falling in love. While the laughs always deliver, I’m invariably awestruck by something else: Amanda’s incredibly chic wardrobe, costume designed by Marlene Stewart.

As a hotshot movie-trailer editor in Hollywood, Amanda has an elegant wardrobe that reads as one word: expensive. Throughout the movie, she almost exclusively wears white, black, and cream. (The latter buttery hue is a Nancy Meyers signature.) While Amanda’s ensembles are devoid of bold colors, prints, or logos, you can just tell that all of the clothes are luxurious—they’re all done in heavy wools and cashmeres, two snuggly materials that simply scream the holidays. It’s basically The Row before The Row was a real thing.

My favorite Amanda look comes at the beginning of the film, when her driver drops her off at her new UK holiday home. She sports an incredible brown trench coat with white shearling trim, complete with a white turtleneck, black skinny-fit trousers, and sky-high stilettos (which she wears in the snow). She then proceeds to cart her three huge suitcases—presumably filled with even more fabulous clothes!—through the snowy terrain up to the house.

As the movie continues, Amanda holds on to her effortlessly chic style. For her first night in the cozy cottage home, she drinks red wine while lounging around in a chunky cream cable-knit sweater, gray sweats, and a lilac beanie, a gray scarf slung effortlessly around her shoulder. (You have to watch her drunkenly sing “Mr. Brightside.”) I’m totally influenced to channel her quietly luxurious approach to style this holiday season, when elevated cozy dressing has its time to shine.

Amanda does deliver a few splashier evening looks in the movie too, should you need inspiration for any upcoming holiday parties. When she pops over for a visit at Jude Law’s home, she arrives wearing an incredible cream coat, unbuttoning it to reveal a black top and cream pencil skirt that’s punctuated with a wide crystal-buckle belt. “I know, I’m a tad overdressed,” she quips. “You look like my Barbie,” Law’s daughter says.

Even Amanda’s approach to formalwear is decidedly sleek and pared back. Her closet basically makes the case for timeless investment pieces: You can clearly still turn heads in a simple but well-cut silhouette. So this holiday season, you’ll find me slipping into my best Nancy Meyers neutrals too. If you find me drunk singing to the Killers at home, though, that’s none of your business.

#6679. We Tried 6 Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies—These Are The Only 2 Worth Serving At Thanksgiving

A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

But sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That said, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

Once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”

Costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

#6676. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6671. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6669. Ciara Has One Holiday Cooking Rule & You Really Don't Want To Break It

She's all for getting creative with Oreos, although she has much stronger feelings about the rest of the menu.

Ciara has one request for whoever’s in charge of Christmas dinner: Please, whatever you do, make sure you’re up for the assignment. She’s willing to embrace a little holiday mess, but apparently, there’s a limit to how far that generosity extends into the kitchen.

“All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”

Ciara, a mom of four, certainly understands how quickly the festivities can get away from you. “Christmas in our house is full of love, excitement and a little chaos,” she said in a statement. But when it comes to the actual Christmas menu, she’s got some traditions she’s pretty attached to, many of which go all the way back to her childhood in Atlanta, Georgia.

"If you know one thing about us ATLians, you have Thanksgiving on Christmas. The same meal comes back around again," she told Delish.

And we’re talking a serious Southern spread: turkey legs, mac and cheese, candied yams, collard greens, chitlins, and pig feet. She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara says those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

#6668. 30 Sparkling, Fringed, and Pleated Holiday Wedding Guest Dresses for Every Festive Fête

Weddings during the holiday season come with a built-in sense of joy. The venue is likely already decked out in garlands and candlelight, everyone is in a celebratory mood, and if the date falls on New Year’s Eve, there’s a midnight countdown baked right into the reception. Your outfit should match that energy. While standard winter guest attire often leans moody, a December through February fête (don’t forget about Valentine’s Day nuptials!) leaves plenty of room to play—think rich textures, high-shine finishes, and statement silhouettes.

As a bridal stylist, I always recommend letting the calendar dictate your palette. A Christmastime wedding begs for jewel tones and seasonal classics like cranberry red, deep emerald, and antique gold—all of which you’ll find at labels like Christopher John Rogers, Posse, and Simkhai. A New Year’s Eve ceremony, on the other hand, calls for anything that catches the light and has movement for the dance floor, from Altuzarra’s gold gown done up in cascading paillettes to Kallmeyer’s swingy fringe. Even a strict black-tie dress code can get a festive upgrade: Trade a standard black gown for a golden lamé maxi courtesy of Ulla Johnson. (Just be sure to check the couple’s wedding website for any specific color requests.)

Of course, a few standard wedding-guest rules still hold true. Steer clear of anything that reads as bridal—that includes winter white, no matter how tempting a cream silk slip might be. Skip the costume-like details, too: A ruby-red J.Crew mini feels spirited, while a tinsel-trimmed ensemble in the same shade can quickly veer kitschy. Beyond that, pay attention to the dress code, as that will dictate your hemline; minis and midis are fair game for less formal invitations, especially when paired with tights and a great heel. And don’t forget about a chic evening coat that’ll tie your outfit together.

Now that you know the basics, it’s time for the fun part. Browse our edit of the 30 best dresses for every holiday wedding on your calendar this winter.

#6666. The Best Eye Makeup to Wear Over 40, From Cream Shadows to Soft Liners

Soft browns and subtle shimmer can define eyes without emphasizing fine lines.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Let’s be clear: there are no age-specific makeup rules. Wear whatever shade or trend you feel best in, no matter your age. That said, it’s no secret that our facial features change as we get older, and to keep looking your best, the skin care and makeup products in your rotation may need to be adjusted accordingly. After 40, that powder eye shadow that once looked perfect across a smooth eyelid may now crease and settle into fine lines. Or your signature eyeliner may have started to look a little less visible because of eyelid hooding. Maybe your lashes are more sparse? Before dumping your entire eye makeup kit, take some cues from a pro on choosing and wearing the best eye makeup after 40.

Before choosing colors, take a look at your current products to assess textures. “As we get older, the skin on our eyelids gets thinner, and a little more crinkled, so heavy or dry powder shadows can settle into fine lines and actually emphasize them,” celebrity makeup artist Brandy Allen tells ELLE. You’ll want to swap out chalky, dry formats for cream-based shadows and liners.

How you treat the skin in your eye area matters too—both for how well and how long the makeup wears. Allen recommends using an eye cream or eye patches to hydrate the skin. “I have been loving the Parivie Smooth & Brighten Eye Masks because of the collagen and skin-loving ingredients they have,” says Allen. “Give the leftover serum a minute to sink in, and then go in with a thin layer of primer like the Urban Decay Eyeshadow Primer Potion so your shadow has something to grip onto and stays crease-free all day,” Allen suggests.

Many hybrid products now combine skin care with color cosmetics. A win-win for aging skin. Look for hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid, smoothing niacinamide, ceramides, and squalene that will treat skin while delivering solid color payoff.

16-hour wear; infused with jojoba esters, ceramides, hyaluronic acid, squalane

Laura Mercier Matte Caviar Stick Eye Shadow

Available in 32 shades; waterproof and sweatproof; formulated with hyaluronic acid and firming raspberry stem cell extract

Comes in 11 colors; buildable; has antioxidant-rich green tea extract and a smoothing natural peptide quinoa extract

A mix of matte, satin, and metallic finishes; formulated with moisturizing jojoba seed oil and antioxidant-rich vitamin E

Look for creamy formulas that blend easily like the M.A.C Dazzleshadow Eye Shadow Stick. These will crease less. “It has a soft metallic shine and 12-hour wear, and it doubles as a liner, so it’s an easy one-step product,” Allen notes.

Satin and soft-sheen finishes are the best here, too. Allen says they give the lid a little luminosity that reflects light, which makes the eye area look more lifted and fresh. “A finely milled shimmer on the center of the lid is great too, especially for the holidays. If you prefer a powder, I love the Jones Road The Best Eyeshadow. It has a soft texture that blends out so easily, and it comes in both matte and shimmer finishes.”

Allen says soft, warm neutrals like taupes, espresso and chocolate browns, bronze, and soft rose gold tones are most flattering for 40 and over eyes. “I’d also recommend swapping a jet-black liner for a deep brown. Brown still defines the eye but looks softer and less harsh against the skin.” Allen’s top pick is the Glampton Cream Eyeshadow & Gel Liner Duo in Espresso & Rose Gold, which she says is a great option here because it gives you both shades in one. “The shadow stick is creaseless, blends out with just your finger, and the gel liner glides on without tugging on the lid,” Allen notes.

Just because your skin is maturing doesn’t mean you can’t try trends. Allen says it’s more about adjusting the trend to work for you. “The lived-in, smudged smoky eye trend is actually great for more mature skin; just keep it soft, and focus the liner on the outer half of the lower lash line instead of going all the way around,” says Allen. One product she suggests avoiding is chunky glitter, as it can settle into lines and emphasize texture.

Once your products are in place, perfect your application technique. It’ll make a difference. “When blending shadow, angle it upward toward the tail of your brow instead of dragging it down. This gives the eye an instant lift,” Allen instructs. You can also tap a little rose gold or champagne shimmer onto the inner corners and center of the lid to brighten. And don’t forget the under-eyes and brows. “A color corrector like the Bobbi Brown Skin Long-Wearing Color Corrector Stick cancels out darkness, and well-groomed, filled-in brows frame the whole eye area,” Allen explains.

#6665. Ina Garten’s Dancing With The Stars Confession Has Me Mourning What Could’ve Been

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

#6663. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6662. Chipotle’s Thanksgiving Eve BOGO Returns For One Night Only—Here's How To Get It

Your Wednesday night plans could use a little extra guac.

Thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before. Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving Eve BOGO deal, giving you a perfectly good excuse to grab a burrito with an old friend before the turkey, stuffing, and inevitable food coma take over.

The deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m. local time at participating U.S. restaurants, with the usual buy one entrée, get one free format we all know and love.

But, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line. You’ll need to be a Chipotle Rewards member, order at the restaurant, and scan your Rewards card at checkout. The free entrée must cost the same as or less than the one you're buying, and you can claim up to five free entrées per check. Kids’ meals don't qualify, and ordering ahead through the app, online, or for delivery won't work.

The timing has changed a bit from last year, too, when it ran from 4 p.m. all the way until closing. This time, you've got a four-hour window, so make sure that one friend you have who’s perpetually late gets the memo.

“The response last year showed us how much our guests embraced the occasion,” Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, said in a statement. According to the chain, the promotion ended up being its biggest sales-driving campaign of 2025, so a return trip was probably inevitable.

And if you’re stuffed and don’t feel like leaving the couch the next day, there’s a little something for the post-Thanksgiving crowd as well. From Friday, November 27, through Monday, November 30, Chipotle is waiving its delivery fee on eligible orders placed through its app or website with code CYBER26. You’ll need to spend at least $10 in the U.S. or $12 in Canada, and delivery menu prices may be higher, with other fees still applying.

If nothing else, it’s a convenient excuse to take a break from the annual challenge of finding increasingly creative ways to eat leftover turkey.

#6661. Inside "The Tupac Tapes" With Radio Legend Angie Martinez

Going back to her early days on New York’s Hot 97, longtime radio host and veteran interviewer Angie Martinez has been getting rappers to drop their guard and engage in revealing, insightful conversations for over 30 years. Hot 97 was where you went to see Angie, Funkmaster Flex and the like if you had a new freestyle to get off, news to break, drama to address. But Martinez didn’t just get scoop; she facilitated dialogues that would often show some of the game’s most furtive rappers entirely at ease. Her show was a destination, her reporting was crucial, and her stature was reflected in a moniker: The Voice of New York.

In the years since, Angie has migrated to Power 105.1 while also moving into the podcast space. But there was always one piece of lore that loomed over her career: she was sitting on an unreleased interview with Tupac Shakur conducted shortly before his death in 1996. Now, 30 years later, she’s ready to pull back the curtain with a four-part podcast on Netflix where she plays the tapes for contemporary hip-hop luminaries like Joe Budden, Charlamagne and Big Boy, as well as figures more directly related to the events in question, like Outlawz member Edi I Mean or Biggie’s right-hand-man Lil Cease.

As the story goes: Pac became a fan of Angie and her work while incarcerated in New York, so much so that after his release he invited her to appear in the music video for his song “I Ain’t Mad at Cha.” Angie refused, and when Pac asked why she explained that a figure so closely associated with the New York rap scene appearing in that video as East Coast-West Coast tensions reached a boiling point could only be a bad look. Pac then invited her to his home to air it all out. So the Voice of New York spent over two hours with Pac hoping to come back with an interview that defused any negative energy. What she got instead was a Pac at his most turnt, angry, hurt, and vengeful, with the rapper saying things about Big, Puffy, and other New York rappers that would’ve only escalated those tensions. So Martinez sat on them, until today.

After viewing all four episodes of the podcast, I connected with Angie to find out why this was the right moment to release the interview, how she assembled such an all-star team of contributors, what she makes of the backlash to her decision, and how the The Tupac Tapes might help our fractured media landscape today.

Yeah, yeah. It's wild, right? You'll have one of those, hopefully. You’ll have a streak.

Yeah, for sure. I wasn't expecting how nostalgic... so much came up for me in [this process] because it's like a time capsule. It's not just Pac's story, but it's my story, it's about media, it's about culturally what we were doing, what we cared about [back then], how we were thinking. Nobody was thinking about healing or fucking trauma. We weren't talking about that type of stuff back then, ever.

It's just interesting to look at these tapes through a modern lens. This little blip, this little moment in history, So anyway, that part was really interesting to do with voices of the culture and people who are actually there. It's just trippy. The best word I can say is “trippy.”

Maybe, and people say that a lot, but back then we honestly weren't thinking about that. At that point in culture, we were just starting to pay attention to SoundScan numbers, we were just starting to pay attention to artists going platinum. There was no understanding of, "I'm going to be an icon." Nobody was thinking about that. We loved this shit. We were happy to be in it. We were trying to figure it out. There was no, “If I put this out, it's going to go viral.” So that's the interesting thing to me.

Yes, it could have been a big moment, but we didn't think like that. And that's the conversation to be had now, in terms of media and what we care about and what's in the front of our brain as we're making decisions and telling stories. How does this land? What's the headline? What are the clips? What’s the spin? Back then it was just like, "I'm going to go there and have this conversation, see what's up." End sentence, end thought.

It was. And the game changed so much and people care about different things now. And I get it. That's what happens with evolution, right? I really went there just to try to get people to hear what Pac was saying to me on the phone: "I don't have a problem at all with New York. That's crazy." And I was like, "Oh, shit. Nobody's heard you say that. I could go get you to say that. It would be so great." And then I go there and, obviously, it's not what he said, and that was not his temperament on that day at that time. So it wasn't a hard decision to make because I didn't want to make this worse when I was actually trying to do the opposite. Also, nobody knew what I had. So it wasn't like a public declaration of, "I'm not going to air it." It was just me quietly deciding [not to].

Well, you heard the tapes, right? The answers are there. It's like, you can hear those tapes and you can understand what would've happened, in that climate and at that time especially, but really at any time. It was sensitive. Things were happening. I mean, nobody had died, but violence was happening, gunfire was happening. So it's not too hard to figure out after you’ve heard the tapes.

Yeah, it's hard to hear. I hate that part so much, but it's what was happening at that moment.

And I'm grateful that I was able to share it with Havoc before it came out and get some context from [Outlawz member] Edi I Mean before putting this out. And that was the whole purpose of me doing it in this type of format. If you put that out with no context, everybody who's looking for a hundred clicks this week now has something. So that's why it was so important for me to do it in this manner.

There's been once or twice where I thought about it and I just didn't see it. I just didn't know how. Quietly, I always knew that it was like an artifact, a piece of history. And Tupac is such an important figure, and this moment in time in hip-hop culture was such an important one that it's part of our history. I'm watching museums go up and stories get told or recounted. And then I'm seeing some narratives about the tapes, things that were not true. And I'm like, “You know what? History is history at the end of the day. So here you go, here's the full history.”

It just took me a little while to figure out how to put them out in a respectful and responsible way. And then once I figured out what that format would be, it happened really quickly, honestly. There was a conversation I had with Charlamagne on my podcast about the tapes. And then it was me sitting down with Brittany, my production partner, like, "All right, if we put these out, who could we have conversations with to give people some understanding?" And then I called Netflix. "I'm going to put these tapes out, but before that I want to have some conversations." They got it right away, and they do a lot of stuff with [production company] All the Smoke, so they paired us with them to help. We made a couple calls, got some people in some chairs, hit play on the tapes, and here we are.

This wasn't, like, five-years-in-the-making. It's not a documentary of Pac's life. I keep saying that because it's important to me for people to know, I am not telling the story of Tupac's life. There's plenty of that in the world and you should go down those rabbit holes. But this story that I decided to tell is about these specific tapes in this very specific time capsule and my experience making them, holding them and then releasing them.

I actually wasn't very close with everyone on the panels. These were just people that I've come across in the business or have had different conversations with and, for different reasons, I thought they had a perspective that would be interesting to hear. Wallo has spent so much time in prison—Pac had just come out of prison and he could speak to what that must have felt like for Pac in that moment. Joe Budden and I have had many conversations about Tupac and he's a prominent voice of our culture. Charlamagne as well. Erica Ford helped Pac come up with the Code of the Streets for Thug Life and still works with his family, but she speaks to that grassroots kind of work also threaded into the conversation as well. E.D., I didn't really know well at all. I had met him the day we did these tapes 30 years ago and I really have had no interaction with him since then. So I was really grateful that he agreed to do it because, number one, he was in the room. And it was also because he was close to Pac, so he could really speak to what was going on with him and how Pac was already changing in real time. Monie Love was important to me and my storytelling because what happened to her when she was in Tha Dogg Pound video had a lot to do with why I didn't want to be in [2Pac’s] “I Ain't Mad at Cha” video and why I ultimately wound up with this interview in the first place.

Other than that, it's people who respond to some of the things he was talking about. Pac was talking about building with groups like Wu-Tang Clan. So I called RZA like, "Did you know that Pac was thinking of this?" And he really didn't. Lil' Cease, there's some things he says here about Big. It really was a labor of love from everybody. This is 30 years later. A lot of forgiveness has happened. A lot of, I don't know, growth has happened. Some of it's uncomfortable, and there was some uncomfortable energy.

Crazy, right? I hear that from people who knew Pac well, that that happens often—that there's a lot of godwinks. The lights went out twice. Through this whole process, there's so many things that have happened. I just left LA last night. I'm sitting in the airport and I just had my appendix taken out. I'm tired, I'm getting prepared to drop this and it's been a crazy couple of weeks making this, creating it, releasing it. And then fucking “I Ain't Mad at Cha” starts playing over the fucking speaker of the fucking airport.

I just sat there by myself laughing. Even the timing: we started [working with Netflix] and then the trial date happened.

Yeah. I kind of separate that stuff, and also that's a documentary. This is different. I really was in the little bubble of this story. Honestly, I didn't include any parts of the trial 'cause that's not the story we're telling. So even though there were things going on, it wasn't part of the tapes. We tried to stay focused on what was on the tapes, which was hard because there are so many interesting things about Pac where I wanted to veer off at different times.There's so many ways you could go. But that was my rule of thumb as a creator.

It was important for me to have other people's opinions, people that put time in, people who have history, people who have earned the right to have opinions.

Thanks, man. I'm always my worst critic. I will always be like, “I could have gone two steps higher. Why didn’t I ask him this?” Or, “I should have gone more into what was going on with Pac emotionally. But I didn't even have the tools to do that at that time.

And I know, because of the nature of the way the media is set up now, that people are going to pick the headlines, and the headlines are going to be the tough stuff. But there's a lot of nuance in there. There's a lot of nuance about him saying he was teaching himself the game, how he didn't have a father figure to show him how to do all this stuff. When I hear him say, “I would be sitting in the cell banging my head against the wall, and not figuratively, but literally banging my head against the wall,” that he has a condition where he was grinding his teeth. I hear that differently now. When I was young, I just wanted him to say, "I don't got beef for the whole coast.” I wasn't hearing what was happening to him as a traumatized man. Imagine—he had been shot five times and he had bullet wounds in his head, and he's in prison banging his head against the wall while he's listening to people on the radio popping champagne and living their best life and going on without him.

But because I'm a crazy person, I'd be like, "Damn, there's 10 other people I would've loved to talk to. I need more time. I need more money. I need more resources." I'm always going to want to tell the story bigger. But I'm just going to have to tell another story next. And that is the plan for IRL Productions. I got a battery in my back right now, for real, a different type of battery in my back. And I know I attribute that to the conversations that we've had and to just being able to get this story out in the manner in which we did.

We could have easily stuck you in one of the chairs. [You and I] did that Sprite panel [earlier this year], all those folks are great. There's plenty of voices of the culture that are doing good work and should be lifted up. So it's not that it doesn't exist. The problem is that the floodgates have opened, and we give the same amount of leverage and the same amount of voice to somebody who puts time and effort into a story and tells a story with care and responsibility as we do some guy who gives no fucks, who's looking for a click.

So that's the problem, but we can't let that stop us from pushing forward and doing what we want to do. I'm not somebody that addresses dumb shit, and I have been very tempted throughout this to jump in and be like, "First of all, you, sir, sound ridiculous." People will say things with absolutely zero truth. And some of them know there's zero truth, but they don't care.

Because you say the word “Tupac,” and you're guaranteed clicks. There were plenty of narratives about what I've done with the tapes, that I’ve sold the tapes. Why would I sell the tapes? I would've made people pay for them if I was trying to get a money grab. There's so many people who just rip it apart. It's the nature of the beast right now. So do I think that there are still people that care? Absolutely. I just hope that the other side of this that makes it so hard doesn't make people not want to do this. It's easy to just be a blood sucker. And I get that, if somebody doesn't know me and my history, they don't know me as a human being, their immediate first thought is to think the worst.

There's a lot of reason to be cynical out here. People do a lot of dumb things for dumb reasons. It's not my business or my job to inform or correct people. It's my business to carry on the way I've been carrying on and to continue to try to tell good stories with responsibility and some integrity.

I love hearing about what his visions were for the future, his plans for hip-hop. But it's not just that. It's him laughing. Sometimes he's on one, and every now and then he'll stop and he'll start laughing and he'll be like, "Nah, you know I didn't mean that like that." When you see him crack a little bit. Like, he’ll be yelling at me, and then he says, "Listen, I'm not mad at you.” Just seeing different sides of him was so interesting and meaningful.

Even when he's saying something that I maybe don't agree with, I really am inspired by his conviction. I am really inspired by his willingness to say what he said, stand on what he believes, tell you exactly how he feels. But he wasn't so far gone that it was this one way. There's a little glimpse into how he was evolving in real time, even inside those tapes. It makes me wish I'd have interviewed him a month later, or two months later, or six months later.

The apartment was lovely. It was brown leather couches. He had a sign that said “Thug Mansion” in his bedroom. I think he also had a home in Malibu, but this was his apartment. He had a picture of him and Janet Jackson from Poetic Justice on the table that was right behind us the whole interview. He was a showman, boy, in every sense of the word. He was a full showman who had a lot of heart, who had a lot of big ideas and passion, and man, I'm grateful to have had that little moment in time with him, for sure.

#6660. Welcome to Wonder by Josh Aronson

Vizcaya is a fantasy, even by Miami standards. I found myself wondering who belongs to it. Here was a forest in the middle of Miami, and beyond it, a house that seemed to have arrived from another time and place. I've always found that meeting a little magical. But I've come to understand how quickly the Florida landscape can change. The longer I spent at Vizcaya, the more I wondered how a photograph might hold some of that feeling, and what it might ask us to protect.

I grew up in South Florida. My family moved here from Toronto when I was three, and we didn't have roots here before us. I've often felt both at home in Miami and curious about my place within it. Vizcaya was part of the city's imagination long before I was invited to make pictures here. To contribute to its story as an artist felt almost difficult to believe.

Photographs have helped shape the way we see Vizcaya from its earliest days. In 1917, Mattie Edwards Hewitt photographed the estate for an issue of Architectural Review devoted to the house and gardens. Her images offered a vision of the world James Deering, Vizcaya's founder, and his collaborators had brought into being on the shore of Biscayne Bay. Today, people come here with cameras for quinceañeras, engagements, weddings, and family portraits. Those pictures find their way into albums and onto walls, carrying a little piece of Vizcaya into homes across Miami.

For Welcome to Wonder, I made a new body of photographs featuring people, animals, and landscapes across Florida. At Vizcaya, the images appear in circular frames around trees and on large banners suspended overhead, along paths that are free to walk seven days a week.

While preparing for Welcome to Wonder, I spent time looking through the estate's archive. In many of the images, people of color appeared working on or caring for the property. I began thinking about what other photographs could exist alongside them: images of young people from Miami's many communities at rest, in play, at ease in the landscape. Who gets to be seen enjoying a place like this? Who gets to imagine that it belongs to them, too?

These questions have been with me throughout my practice, from Tropicana to Florida Boys. I've traveled the state with groups of young men, making photographs in springs, swamps, forests, and along backroads. Many of us grew up in Miami and were encountering these places together for the first time. I would arrive with an idea for a scene, but the pictures were shaped by the people who came along and what the landscape offered us. I've returned to places I'd scouted and found a body of water had dried up or a shoreline had shifted. Those changes stay with me. The places that feel so expansive and enduring can be fragile, too.

I think often about Naomi Fisher's Cibachromes and Hernan Bas' paintings, the tension and theatricality their subjects seemed to find together in the landscape. Those photographs and paintings helped me imagine what it might mean to create a new world with other people, and make an image of it. With Florida Boys, I wanted to picture young men who could be tender with one another, who could rest, who could be curious. Making the photographs gave us a reason to go out and experience something together. What began as an imagined scene became part of our lives.

At Vizcaya, that world began to grow. I found myself wondering what might have happened if, after Deering died, a band of young people had moved into the estate. Who would they have loved? What would their days have looked like? What would they have discovered in the trees and along the water? I began to see the photographs as a kind of fictional archive, evidence of encounters that might have taken place here. Some pictures were made at Vizcaya; others were made elsewhere in South Florida. Together, they allowed me to imagine a landscape without the boundaries of a single property or moment in time.

For this project, I also photographed young mothers, young fathers, and young families. I thought about the lives a photograph can have after it is made. A child might one day look at an image and see their parent as a young person. A mother might see something of her own family in the gesture of someone she has never met. The photograph becomes a kind of mirror, reflecting something different depending on who we are and where we stand in our lives. I hope these pictures hold a little of that possibility for the people in them, the way they do for me.

I thought, too, about Deering. He never married, and questions about his sexuality have followed him long after his death. The historical record doesn't give us a conclusive answer. As an artist, I'm interested in the space between what a life contains and what the archive preserves. We do know that Paul Chalfin, Vizcaya's artistic director, lived here with his partner, Louis Koons. I wonder about the other private worlds that might have existed here, leaving traces we may never find.

On the Hammock Paths, photographs printed on acrylic are held in circular frames that appear to float around the trees. Along the Metrorail route, larger images hang in the canopy, printed on mesh that lets the light filter through. I was thinking about the symmetry of Vizcaya's gardens, but also about the way a circle has no beginning and no end. You can walk around a ring and find a photograph on either side. You can enter the path from the city or come upon it as you leave the museum. The images can be discovered, passed by, returned to, seen differently on any day.

Both the Hammock Paths and the Metrorail site are free and open to the public seven days a week. You don't need a ticket to spend time with the work. In a city where so much can feel out of reach, that matters. I think about the people who walk these paths every day, on their way home or with a dog, and the people who might encounter the photographs without knowing anything about Florida Boys or my collaborators. The possibility that an image could become part of someone's daily life feels like a gift and a responsibility.

Across the city, at MOCA, my commission A Sudden Leap rises from the plaza's reflecting pool. Four photographs of Florida's natural world have become sails, suspended above the water. Some of these quieter images grew out of the same journeys that gave me Florida Boys. There are no people in the pictures, but there are people moving around them, bringing their own histories and experiences to the work. I think about the sails and the journeys that have brought so many of us to Miami, including my own family. I hope the photographs might make someone want to see these places and care about what happens to them.

To have work at Vizcaya and at MOCA, my neighborhood museum, at the same time is something I'm still trying to take in. Both have given me a way to look at the place that raised me, and to offer those images back to the people who live here. The photographs at Vizcaya will eventually come down, and people will continue to walk these paths. I hope someone remembers an image the next time they pass a tree, or carries a little of the feeling of this place back into the city with them. What we choose to see, I've come to believe, has something to do with what we choose to hold dear.

Josh Aronson's Welcome to Wonder is on view at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, Miami through May 24, 2027. A Sudden Leap, Aronson's MOCA Art on the Plaza public artwork commission, is on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami through January 17, 2027.

Josh Aronson (b. 1994, Canada) is a Miami-based artist whose work explores masculinity and landscape in the American South.
