#6658. Ina Garten Makes A Pretty Convincing Case For Thanksgiving Over Christmas

The Barefoot Contessa knows exactly what she wants out of a holiday.

Christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just showed up with string beans.”

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

"Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

It makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

#6656. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6654. The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

The simplest Thanksgiving side deserves better.

In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so important. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

In the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a big batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

#6653. Santiago Lastra Wants You to Stop Overthinking Mexican Food

Santiago Lastra might have become a mathematician if it weren’t for a box of Ritz crackers. Growing up in Cuernavaca, Mexico, the future chef behind London restaurants KOL and Fonda was the sort of kid with more of an appetite for national math competitions. “There would be four questions and five hours to answer those four questions,” he remembers. “I loved that. I wanted to do that for the rest of my life.”

Then, at 15, Lastra spotted a crab dip recipe on the back of a cracker box. He made it for his family and watched as an ordinary day changed shape around something he had cooked. “I became obsessed with the idea that you can create a special occasion just by cooking something for someone,” he says. The mathematical brain moved into the kitchen. In his first cookbook, Mexican Soul: A New Style of Cooking, Lastra writes about the magic of both disciplines: starting with a few ingredients (or figures) and a recipe (or equation) and creating something greater than the sum of its parts.

The chef has spent the past month touring the U.S. in support of the book: He’s made tacos at New York’s Santo Taco, cooked at Yucatan-style seafood spot Holbox in Los Angeles, and enlisted The Bear’s Will Poulter to put a Mexican spin on the Italian beef sandwich at Chicago’s storied Mr. Beef (the real-life inspiration for the show’s original restaurant). Along the way, he’s helped introduce American audiences to a philosophy of Mexican cooking that is as resourceful and intuitive as it is traditional and communal.

It’s an instinct that has taken Lastra on a circuitous journey back home. He started out cooking Italian food, then left Mexico for kitchens in Spain. Various fascinations with French techniques, the experimentalism of Mugaritz, and New Nordic cuisine followed. “As a young kid, when you leave Mexico, you feel that you made it,” he says. “It took me a long time to realize that what we had in Mexico was really the answer.” Lastra began applying Mexican techniques to local ingredients in Scandinavia, then traveled and cooked across 27 countries. Returning to Mexico to work on Noma’s Tulum pop-up allowed him to look at his homeland with newly curious eyes. “Being Mexican became my superpower,” he says. “I was able to share culture through food, and it opened the doors to the world for me.”

KOL was his attempt to make that realization tangible: the Marylebone restaurant that Lastra opened in 2020 cooks Mexican food through seasonal British ingredients. Fonda, its more casual and rambunctious sibling, followed four years later. “I wanted KOL to be one of the best restaurants in the world,” he says, to prove “that Mexican food should be recognized at the level of all the best cuisines in the world.” Not everyone Lastra hoped to touch could ever make it to his London spots or the global pop-ups. “What really makes a difference culturally is the food that people do at home,” he says. “Home cooking is more personal.”

Mexican Soul posed some questions. How do you cook food that feels fundamentally Mexican without fresh masa, the right dried chillies, or a specialist grocer? Lastra didn’t want readers buying a two-pound bag of chipotle for one dinner. “I had to change the way I think,” he says. He began writing new rules for the weeknight home cook, rather than an ingredients-led chef. The transition required its own education. He pored over British supermarket aisles, and during a family beach vacation, Lastra locked himself inside to watch hours of Jamie Oliver. He and his brother Eduardo, his collaborator on the book and at KOL, went into a supermarket and decreed that nothing for the shoot could be ordered elsewhere.

“It tasted great,” he recalls. “I was like, wow… I think I’ve been overcomplicating myself all my life.” Just like in his childhood math competitions, limitations could provide the route to a more interesting solution. The book’s first half teaches some culinary grammar: Sourness, heat, sweetness, smoke, fat, and masa are defined and built into pillar dishes such as guacamole and quesadillas to demonstrate how those sensations work together. “Every time I create a dish, I always see flavors,” Lastra explains. “They’re like your paintings, your colors.”

The second half gets freer: tomato and cherry aguachile, potato rajas tamales, asparagus pipián. Innovating beyond traditional Mexican cooking, this style is rooted in the cuisine’s history and designed to work with seasonal, local, and accessible ingredients from wherever its cook lives. Lastra resists the idea of Mexican food as something stuck in amber. “The most beautiful thing about Mexican cooking, or Mexican food and Mexican culture in general, is that it keeps evolving,” he says. His proudest—and most last-minute addition—was a tortilla. Nearly defeated by the challenge of creating one without corn masa, Lastra had the novel idea of using mashed potato. Combining it with potato starch, he pressed and cooked the dough, and after days of tweaking, “suddenly it worked and it puffed!” It made it into the book just before printing.

Home-testing in the Lastra household has been even sweeter. After we speak, Lastra’s mother—who almost never cooks—is making the book’s mackerel a la Veracruzana for her sons. She’s already sending photographs as she shops for ingredients. “I think she’s never cooked a specific recipe from a cookbook in her life,” he says. “So that’s going to be such a highlight.”

Below, Santiago Lastra’s recipe for albóndigas and Mexican rice, two ways.

Meatballs came to Mexico from the Middle East during the colonial period. They’re a classic of central Mexican home cooking, and are also served in casual eateries called fondas, where they are served with rice and bread or tortillas. The sauces they are served with vary from loose sauces made with cooked green tomatillos to rich tomato and guajillo chilli-based broths. I serve mine in a tomato caldillo with Mexican rice—a classic from our hometown. This is one of my favorite Mexican dishes, and one I would often choose to make if I am hosting friends for dinner.

Red rice is present at most lunches for any Mexican growing up, whether at home or eaten in a fonda. The preparation is simple: rice with peas and carrots, cooked in a tomato and chilli caldillo. The result is a spicy, umami rice with a beautiful color. Serve with stews and tortillas.

Like the red version, this preparation adds a bit of spice, texture, and umami to plain rice. It’s served with all sorts of stews and other dishes in central Mexico, and also with broths like chicken consomé—the kind your mom might make for you when you’re unwell. Fresh jalapeños add a beautiful spicy finish. Perfect with chicken or any other proteins and refried beans.

#6652. ELLE Escapes: London

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

A trip to London may conjure two different and somewhat competing vacation fantasies: the first, a more royal-inspired vision, with fancy tea parties, shopping at Selfridges, and photos outside Kensington Palace, and the second somewhat grungier, filled with smoky Camden bars and vinyl shopping in Soho. Why not do both? For ELLE Escapes, we compiled some of our favorite spots for making the most of your journey across the pond. London’s calling—here’s where to eat, drink, stay, and shop when you answer.

There’s no better way to see London than riding along the Thames itself. The Tower of London offers its own 40-minute river cruise on the country’s first electric passenger boat. Sit back, relax, and listen as the boat’s lively guide breaks down the backstory of the city’s famed bridges and buildings—and takes any questions you have about the city’s history. Bad weather isn’t an issue aboard this ship, thanks to its see-through canopy roof and indoor section. Want to see London at its absolute best? Try booking after sunset during the cooler months so you can take in the city’s lights.

In 2000, Swedish supergroup ABBA famously turned down a $1 billion offer to reunite. Now, thanks to cutting-edge technology, you can see them together again—sort of. ABBA Voyage is a first-of-its-kind live show featuring digital versions of Agnetha Fältskog, Björn Ulvaeus, Benny Andersson, and Anni-Frid Lyngstad, performing alongside a live 10-piece band at their custom-built ABBA Arena in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, London. It’s truly an experience like no other.

A trip here never feels complete without a bit of vintage shopping. Picture this: you’re wandering through Hackney when a pair of vintage Issey Miyake cropped cargos catches your eye in the window. Step inside and you’ll discover Files London, a concept archive store in East London that feels like a true treasure trove. Specializing in Japanese, French, British, Belgian, and Italian designers, the shop offers a meticulously curated selection that fashion lovers will swoon over. The space itself is just as striking as the clothes, making the visit an experience in its own right. And while this city is brimming with vintage and thrift gems, a stop at Files pairs perfectly with an afternoon of shopping in nearby Shoreditch or Soho. Pro tip: bring an extra bag—or at least leave some room in your suitcase—for all the new finds.

It’s not a visit to London without afternoon tea, and Pan Pacific London’s offering truly raises the bar. The meal starts with the server unfolding and placing your napkin on your lap, a British tradition. Then comes the amuse-bouche course with its standout pork and apricot sausage roll. The sandwich course follows—four different types, with the menu changing seasonally—along with a palate cleanser (a cold jasmine infusion in the summer) before the sweets take center stage. First, you’ll munch on scones with clotted cream, citrus curd, and jam. But save room for the grand finale: a gorgeous array of four small pastries. For those in town for the holidays, the Christmas tea includes a mini yule log and a coconut snowman macaron that’s almost too adorable to eat. Almost.

Your culinary experience isn’t complete without a Sunday roast. For that and a whole lot more, try The Grill at The Dorchester, a landmark restaurant that first opened its doors in 1931. Expect modern takes on classic fare—including but not limited to a carving trolley. (We’re salivating too.)

Located on the 60th floor of one of London’s tallest buildings in Mayfair, Gordon Ramsay’s new Asian-inspired restaurant Lucky Cat offers a feast for the eyes as much as for the stomach. Dine alongside panoramic views of the city, which really stand out at night. For those hungry but unsure where to begin with the restaurant’s extensive options, Lucky Cat offers three different tasting menus. Notable dishes include its yellowtail tartare topped with caviar and yuzu, along with its melt-in-your-mouth grilled miso salmon and tender scallops with yuzu and sweet corn. Don’t skip dessert; the mango cheesecake, designed to be a trompe l’œil of the fruit with its white chocolate shell, is a light but special way to cap off a decadent meal.

By Malene Birger Blanca Fringed Boucle Cardigan

By Malene Birger Belicia Fringed Mini Skirt

Mr. Lyan (bartender Ryan Chetiyawardana’s nom célèbre) knows how to make a good cocktail, be it at Washington, D.C.’s Silver Lyan or London’s Lyaness. The U.K. outpost, tucked into South Bank’s Sea Containers building, has some of the most innovative drinks you’ll find in the city, all with cheeky backstories written on the menu for you to discover. While the bar’s offerings do change, the Rainwater Fix was one of its best from its Collaboration 2.0 menu. The tropical mixture, featuring Patrón blanco tequila (or Tropic All in its mocktail version), pineapple shio, Capreolus eau de vie, and passion fruit wine, will transport you back to summer with one sip—no matter what the weather is outside. There’s also plenty of food to enjoy, like sea bass ceviche tacos, fries, and English coastal oysters served with a black currant mignonette.

Fitz’s, named after the hotel’s original architect, is a cocktail bar that turns drinking into a playful experience. Inside, a striking, contemporary interior nods to the hotel’s historic roots, while a unique UV-light menu adds a theatrical twist. With inventive cocktails and attentive service, Fitz’s is an ideal spot for a pre-dinner drink or a stylish night out in Bloomsbury.

It’s not a wild night out in London if you don’t, at some point, find yourself in Shoreditch—and Tonight Josephine is the perfect stop for maximalists in search of an Instagrammable end to the evening. The décor channels early-aughts club life, complete with lots of hot pink, neon signs, and—naturally—a photo booth.

Hyde Park is easily one of the most beautiful places in central London—so why not stay at an iconic hotel with panoramic views of it? The Royal Lancaster London, a member of Preferred Hotels & Resorts, spans 18 floors and features 411 rooms that blend timeless elegance with modern comfort. Following a $115 million renovation, the hotel now boasts sleek, light-filled interiors, marble bathrooms, rainfall showers, and a warm, welcoming atmosphere. Book a deluxe room or suite for wraparound windows offering a vantage point that stretches from Wembley Stadium to the Shard. Perfectly positioned on the edge of Hyde Park, the hotel puts you within walking distance of some of London’s top destinations—Knightsbridge and Harrods across the park, or Oxford Street and Marble Arch just 15 minutes away on foot.

Kimpton Fitzroy blends historic grandeur with playful modernity. From its terracotta-adorned façade to the moody marble archways and astrological-tiled floors, the hotel evokes a mythical, storied past. Step inside the rooms, and the atmosphere transforms—each suite is uniquely styled, combining contemporary design with whimsical details. It’s the kind of place that feels like a home away from home. The location is a dream for avid explorers: perched on Russell Square in the heart of Bloomsbury, the hotel offers easy access to the British Museum, Oxford Street, boutique shops in Soho, and more. Harry Potter fans are just minutes from Platform 9¾, while a short bus ride north will take you to Primrose Hill, where the iconic scene from One Day was filmed.

Nestled in the stunning former Whiteleys department store building, Six Senses London is far more than just a beautiful place to wake up in Bayswater. The hotel is dedicated to your wellness—be it in the small details like its pillow menu and “ginger hello” check-in treats (including its locally sourced ginger kombucha and chocolate orange truffles) or bigger ones like its innovative spa, where the team will craft a plan to help your body best recover based on your key biomarker readings, using the facility’s 13 treatment rooms. While there’s plenty to explore in the picturesque Kensington Gardens and Notting Hill nearby, there’s a good reason to stay in, too. Standout experiences include booking an appointment at the alchemy bar, where a skilled herbalist will make you a tea or tonic to address any health concerns, and having a leisurely dinner at the hotel’s Whiteley’s Kitchen. The produce-driven restaurant has an incredible “Trust the Chef” tasting menu where thoughtful dishes like mushroom tagliatelle with coffee butter and butterflied sea bass with sea fennel will enchant you with every bite.

AKT London The Haze: A Deodorizing Body Mist

If you own an AKT deodorant, you know the brand doesn’t skimp on delectable scents. Its deodorizing mists are no different, using the same deodorant formula to keep you fresh and smelling good from head to toe.

Violette Fr Lip Nectar Hydrating Lip Stain

Skip the constant touch-ups and opt for a formula that looks good at the start, middle, and end of your day. Lips look visibly plump and juicy, thanks to a hyaluronic acid and squalane base.

Yves Saint Laurent Libre Santal Couture Eau de Parfum

At the base of Libre Santal is sandalwood, which transforms this perfume into a deep, sensual woody aroma. It has its bright moments at first, with a soft lavender and orange blossom opening. As it settles, it feels warmer and cozier, perfect for London’s chilly days and nights.

Additional reporting by Claire Stern Milch and Leah Romero.

#6651. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6650. IHOP Is Bringing Its First-Ever Collectible Coffee Mug To Restaurants This Holiday Season

It’s getting increasingly difficult to keep up with all the limited-edition tumblers, advent calendars, and seasonal releases that disappear off shelves before you’ve finished your morning coffee. And now IHOP is giving breakfast lovers another reason to make room in their kitchen cabinets.

Delish can exclusively reveal that IHOP is launching its first-ever Collector's Holiday Mug on Monday, November 30, with the mugs being sold at participating restaurants nationwide. It’s also the very first time the pancake chain has ventured into selling merchandise directly to customers—and, as it turns out, the idea has been brewing for quite some time.

According to Samantha Strong, IHOP’s executive director of brand calendar strategy, the company has heard from enough coffee-loving customers over the years to realize there was an actual appetite for owning an IHOP mug. “What started as a frequent question has grown into a genuine fan obsession,” she said, and this holiday release is now the company's first attempt to turn that enthusiasm into something people can actually buy.

IHOP says coffee is its second best-selling menu item, which means an awful lot of people have spent their mornings clutching one of those mugs while waiting for breakfast. But before you start planning an entire IHOP-themed kitchen makeover, know that each participating location will have just 24 (yes, only 24!) mugs available. Once they're gone, they’re gone, at least as far as this limited-time release is concerned.

There's certainly no shortage of things to collect this holiday season, but at least this one’s something you can actually put to use while doing some damage to a stack of pancakes.

The Levi’s Black Friday Sale is easy money. #6646. The Best Cold-Weather Cocktails to Drink This Holiday Season

I typically take a less-is-more approach when it comes to my beverage choices. Having been burned one too many times by the flavor-packed ‘ingenuity’ of a bar’s signature cocktail, I’ve come to the conclusion that a martini, Negroni, or gin and tonic are better suited to my spartan palate. But once the holidays roll around, well, my fidelity to simplicity goes out the window, and I am an enthusiastic proprietor of the cozy cocktail.

What’s a cozy cocktail? Exactly what you think it is. A spirited sip that summons the mood of a crackling fireplace and the flavors of a Christmas kitchen. That transports you to a snowed-in cabin in Lapland, or a bustling holiday market in Germany. And I’m not talking about kitschy cocktails afflicted by crushed-up candy canes and artificial syrups—no, no. These are recipes that chase the outer limits of mixology, bringing together all that is merry and bright and elegantly transmuting it into your glass.

There are many paths a cold-weather cocktail may take. Traditional classics, like eggnog and hot toddies, are always welcome. For something theatrical, a smoked tipple does the trick (top marks for those performed tableside). For an off-the-charts cozy cocktail, those infused with seasonal spices will leave you deliriously jolly. And if you can’t bear to part ways with your old fashioned or espresso martini, take solace in knowing there are ways to ‘winter-fy’ these quintessential favorites.

If you’re ready to raise a glass of something cozy in the coming weeks, let the guide below inform your order. And for those who wish to whip up cocktails for a festive fête at home, don’t miss the recipes at the end. Bar carts at the ready!

The holidays present a decadent array of creamy cocktails calibrated specifically for the season. Take eggnog, for example. This rich tipple originated from a hot, milky, ale-adjacent drink called ‘posset’ that was enjoyed during Britain’s medieval era. Somewhere along the timeline, eggs joined the party, and several hundred years later, we’ve arrived at our modern-day recipes that consist of milk, heavy whipping cream, sugar, eggs, and nutmeg (spiked with rum, bourbon, or brandy). A boozy holiday milkshake, if you like.

Over at Smithereens in the East Village, head bartender Jacob Dorman wanted to make an eggnog with their in-house label rum, but decided to do an egg flip variation to show the versatility of the rum. (For reference, the main difference between an egg flip and eggnog is that a traditional flip leaves the dairy out.) “People always think of rum as a tropical spirit, but it can be warming and comforting too,” Dorman says. He uses a squash amaro for his flip, which “is like drinking pumpkin pie (in a good way).”

Another creamy drink that foregoes the use of eggs is coquito. This Puerto Rican holiday cocktail typically uses coconut milk, cream of coconut, evaporated milk, sweetened condensed milk, vanilla extract, cinnamon, and ground nutmeg—spiked with rum. In a similar spirit, at The Wig Shop in Boston, beverage director Oscar Simoza is currently serving up a Venezuelan-inspired take on eggnog. It’s made with banana peel-infused rum, batido de cambur (ripe banana and milk), and arequipe (caramelized milk). Notes of anise and cinnamon, alongside a hint of amaro, come together for a cocktail that is sublimely silky.

The Brandy Alexander is another perennial classic. It’s made with brandy or cognac, dark crème de cacao, heavy cream, and freshly grated nutmeg for garnish. One of my favorite variations is at Bar Rêve in Cobble Hill. “Ours is an après-ski homage,” co-founder Victor Triebel says. They pair a base of cognac with a layer of Frangelico whipped cream, finished with freshly grated nutmeg. “There’s nothing more luxurious than a warming brandy cocktail to end the evening,” Triebel adds.

During the chilliest months of the year, a cocktail encircled by fragrant smoke is just what the doctor ordered. Last winter, I found myself in the grand lobby of the Carlton Hotel St. Moritz, where drinks are served beside a stone fireplace and arrive via trolley cart. Their Piz Nair Mule—presented in a glass case—is inspired by a mountain that rises 3,057 meters above the Engadin Valley. Once the case is opened, a gentle cloud of smoke escapes, revealing the cocktail and miniature alpine landscape, complete with a moss-covered mountain and tiny mountaineers traversing the summit. The cocktail itself is a soothing blend of fresh thyme and rosemary, spicy ginger, and lime.

If you can’t make it all the way to Switzerland this year, fret not, because San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, California, has an entire menu dedicated to its tableside smoked cocktails. I’ve had the Smoking Pig Poke, which combines rye whiskey, averna, Luxardo maraschino, and a bacon-wrapped brandied cherry—all smoked with cherry wood. (They also serve cocktails smoked with oak, hickory, pecan, and pear woods—in case you’re picky about such things.) And if you’d like to impress your friends and try your hand at your own smoked cocktails, this smoke infuser would make an excellent holiday gift.

Distilling the holiday season’s rich baking spices into a cocktail is nothing short of alchemy. Cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, cardamom, allspice—each offers its own shade of warmth, and can be used as liquor infusions, spiced syrups, bitters, or simply garnishes.

At the newly opened Thai restaurant, Hommali, head bartender Patrick Cura created their Horchata Oolong cocktail, blending tequila, shochu, and sweet vermouth that’s been infused with oolong and umami bitters. “We torch a cinnamon stick over the glass for the garnish so you get an initial hit of baking spice at the first sip,” he shares. “It feels like a warm hug in a glass, which is particularly enjoyable when the temps start to drop.”

Over at The Portrait Bar inside The Fifth Avenue Hotel, bar director Darryl Chan’s Marrakesh cocktail is inspired by the spice markets of Morocco. And further downtown at abcV in the Flatiron District, the Saffron Mylk rum cocktail is a blend of spices and saffron, heated with oat milk and honey, then finished with lashings of nutmeg. “The aroma from the nutmeg gives a wonderful warmth, with the heady spice evoking the holidays,” Chris Moore, director of beverage at Jean-Georges Restaurants, says.

And if you’re searching for something a bit lighter, head for Williamsburg dive Shenanigans for their spiced vodka cran, featuring vodka, mulled wine with baking spices, lemon, and soda. (Starting December 2, Shenanigans will kick off their holiday pop-up serving festive cocktails through the new year—make haste.)

While the holidays have spurred legendary cocktail creations aplenty, if you prefer to stick to what you know, look for seasonal riffs on the classics. Hot cocoa is a wonderful place to start. You can spike your beloved hot chocolate with everything from aged rum and bourbon to cointreau and Bailey’s Irish cream. At Limo Bar in the East Village, their Santa’s Coffee cocktail dials up the cozy by pairing Irish whiskey and coffee with maple syrup and salted maple cream.

On a recent visit to the newly opened Bar CC, I ordered the Vesuvio, which is their spin on a coffee Boulevardier. The cocktail layers coffee-infused bourbon with cacao, tonic bean, amontillado sherry, Barolo Chinato, Campari, and Cappelletti rosso. The cocktail is then clarified with heated milk that’s been enriched with mascarpone. (Professional mixology here; do not attempt at home.) But wait! I haven’t even arrived at the best part: an edible lace doily is delicately draped over the glass, resulting in the most elegant riff on a Boulevardier you or I have ever encountered.

For the espresso martini devout among us, head for Pinky Swear to order the Cloud 9, which is an espresso martini garnished with a torched marshmallow. Or if you’re an old fashioned fanatic, take note of the Outtake at New Orleans’s Cure bar, which is seasoned with warm walnut and crisp ginger. Even clear spirits can receive the holiday treatment—at Dandelion in the West Village, their Poire None cocktail swirls together tequila, mezcal, ginger, allspice, yellow Chartreuse, and pear cider for an autumnal riff on the timeless mule. And at Dean’s, rather than relying on brandy or whiskey to conjure the cozies, their winter-friendly take on a classic sbagliato features sloe gin and elderflower liqueur for a deeper, fruitier character.

When in doubt, if you have a go-to cocktail but want to get into the spirit of the season, ask your bartender what they’ve got up their sleeve.

Not drinking alcohol? There are plenty of cozy mocktails that still fit the prompt. Beverages like eggnog, coquito, hot toddies, and hot chocolate can all be created with as much depth and complexity as their boozy counterparts—just skip the liquor part at the end. The Pear of Aces at Golden Steer is an aromatic hot toddy that simmers whole cloves, cinnamon, and star anise with lush pear nectar and melted lemon sherbet.

Or there’s the spirit-free amaretto sour at The Lobby Bar inside Hotel Chelsea, which doubles down on roasted flavors. This cocktail uses a zero-proof Amaretto liqueur made of roasted almonds from Puglia, plus a roasted green tea that’s acidified with lemon juice. “The cocktail is served up with a floater of honey-miso whipped cream, to replicate the head of egg white foam from a traditional sour-style cocktail,” shares Brian Evans, the director of bars at Sunday Hospitality.

Throwing a holiday party and need a few cozy cocktail ideas? Continue below for libations that will get everyone into the spirit of the season.

Directions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a coupe and garnish with grated chocolate.

“The Grasshopper is usually credited to Tujague's in New Orleans. It's a simple drink: crème de menthe, crème de cacao, and a splash of Franca menta and fresh cream, shaken until frothy and served a cool, pale green. Mint and chocolate taste like candy canes and peppermint bark, and the cream makes it smooth and soft. The green looks right at home by a tree or under twinkling lights. It's light and festive, a little nostalgic, and closer to dessert in a glass than to a cocktail” - Linden Pride, principal, Dante Elizabeth Street

Directions: Run the apples through an extractor to separate the juice from the solids, letting the juice pour directly into a frothing pitcher. Add the sauce and bourbon. Steam all ingredients with a steam wand as though preparing milk for a latte. Pour into a heated mug.

Toddy Sauce Directions: Toast eight cinnamon sticks and four grams of whole black pepper in a pot. Add 650 grams Lambic (Duchess de Bourgogne), 650 grams Maple syrup, 12 grams turmeric and nine grams black pepper. Bring to a quick boil then lower to a simmer for 10 minutes. Cool and strain into a deli.

“Fresh pressed green apples are some of my favorite things to work with because the texture is so frothy coming out of the Breville. Steaming them doubles down on the intensity of the technique. The spice blend of turmeric, black pepper, and cinnamon evokes strong winter memories without falling into ‘pumpkin spice’ or Angostura bitters. Everything remains both familiar and impossibly new.” - Owen Gibler, Beverage Director, Bar Roza

Directions: Beat egg yolks and sugars until lightened in color and texture. In a separate bowl, combine dairy, spirits, salt, and nutmeg. Slowly stream the mixture into the beaten egg yolks and sugar while mixing. Once homogeneous, transfer to a sterile glass container and refrigerate for at least one week, ideally one month. Serve with freshly grated nutmeg.

“An elevated take on the holiday classic, Beckon’s Aged Eggnog is prepared months in advance, allowing bonded bourbon, Armagnac, aged and white rum to mellow alongside egg yolks, cream, milk, sugar and nutmeg. Aged for at least one week (though a month is even better), the high-proof spirits develop an almost cheesecake-like tang, resulting in a rich, warming cocktail finished simply with freshly grated nutmeg.” - Joseph Buckley, beverage director, Paired Hospitality

#6644. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6643. People Are Calling The Day Before Thanksgiving ‘Green Wednesday’—And It’s Becoming A Huge Holiday

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting roasted.

Thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

If you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly announces they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery company Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence company BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

According to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The company’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok users sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

As Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those users, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

Americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an important reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

#6642. Kit Keenan & Gigi Powers’s Mom’s Feta Artichoke Dip

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

Alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being quickly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. The brine from the canned artichoke hearts allows the feta to melt down in the oven, which in turn coats the artichoke hearts, creating a velvety dip. The best part about this recipe is that it’s completely customizable. My favorite variation includes adding honey, thyme, and an olive topper, which elevates the dip to a whole new level. Serve it with crunchy crostini or pita chips at your next dinner party, and your guests will go crazy.

Jennifer Aniston has kept her love life largely out of the public eye since her 2018 split from Justin Theroux, but that appears to be changing. In July 2025, the Friends star was photographed vacationing in Mallorca, Spain, with Jim Curtis, a wellness expert whose résumé spans everything from hypnotherapy to roles at major health platforms. Days later, People and Us Weekly confirmed that Aniston and Curtis were dating.

Things became more serious, and on Nov. 2, 2025, Aniston went Instagram official with her partner. She later spoke about him in her ELLE Women in Hollywood interview, calling him “quite extraordinary.” Below, everything to know about Curtis.

Curtis refers to himself as a “wellness pioneer, author, and coach,” on his official website. His approach blends subconscious work, mindfulness, and spiritual coaching to help people “break free from their past to create an entirely new, empowered reality.”

Curtis’s background includes roles at WebMD and Everyday Health. He now works as a transformational coach and speaker, offering services he calls “hypno-realizations.”

Curtis’s focus on healing is personal. At 22 years old, he was diagnosed with lesions on his spinal cord, which led to years of chronic pain, muscle spasms, and mobility issues. “It was unknown how they started, but I very rapidly became ill and soon had trouble walking,” he said in a 2018 interview with Fast Company.

“My own illness and disability forced me to confront the limited beliefs, disconnection, and trauma that were keeping me sad, sick, and alone,” Curtis writes on his website. “Through many powerful tools, including hypno-realization, I not only transformed my physical health, depression, and relationships, but I’ve also helped thousands of others break free to create an entirely new reality full of connection, community, and love.”

Curtis has written two books: The Stimulati Experience (2017), which outlines nine principles for overcoming pain and setbacks, and Shift: Quantum Manifestation Guide (2024), coauthored with Sara Hadir.

In May 2025, Aniston shared a photo of one of Curtis’s books in an Instagram carousel, tagging him in the post.

Curtis has cultivated a strong online presence, posting manifestation exercises and motivational videos for over 550,000 followers. His content regularly covers themes like emotional resilience, moving on from heartbreak, and building self-worth. Some of his past clients include Miranda Kerr and Julianne Hough.

Beyond coaching, Curtis is the co-founder of UFACTORY, a branding firm that helps creators and entrepreneurs grow their digital identities. The company’s mission, per its website, is to build “creator, entrepreneur, and CEO personas that attract loyal fandoms and supercharge revenue opportunities.”

Curtis and Aniston were first spotted together at the luxury resort Ventana Big Sur in California.

In July, they were photographed again in Mallorca, alongside Aniston’s longtime friends Jason Bateman and his wife, Amanda Anka. Aniston appeared to be introducing Curtis to the couple before they boarded a yacht.

While the Mallorca trip brought their rumored romance into the public eye, Aniston and Curtis connected before. Aniston reportedly followed Curtis on Instagram for nearly two years and had liked numerous posts on topics such as healing, affirmations, and relationships.

In April, she told Travel + Leisure that she’d recently begun using hypnosis to overcome her fear of flying, though she didn’t mention Curtis by name. “But I have been doing some hypnosis lately...it’s shockingly good!” she said.

Other slides featured pics of her spending time with friends, including Courteney Cox, Sandra Bullock, Sean Hayes, and Adam Sandler.

On September 10, Curtis stepped out with Aniston at the season 4 premiere of The Morning Show. Aniston walked the carpet on her own in a simple black gown, with Curtis standing nearby as she posed for photos.

He continued, “So start now. Go out, open yourself to love. Make eye contact and smile. Connect with people, and most importantly, love yourself. When you love yourself, you will magnetize more love to you.”

On November 2, Aniston celebrated Curtis’s birthday by posting a black-and-white image of them on Instagram with the caption, “Happy birthday my love. Cherished ❤️”

A source speaking with People on Nov. 15, 2025, shared an update on their connection.

“She acts like she feels very safe with him. She’s really in a great place,” said the source. “They both liked little rituals and moments that are grounding. They are both into symbolism.”

#6639. The Best Christmas Rom-Coms of the 2000s

Name a better feeling than this: you’ve got a plate of picky bits piled high, a glass of fizz in hand, a fire on, your phone Bricked, and a film you’ve seen one hundred times lined up. Winter gets a bad rap, for many reasons, but this Christmas scene? A true flow state.

For some reason, Christmas is the only time of year when we’re not just willing to watch films we could recite by heart while half-asleep—it seems to be a centerpiece of the holiday.

For many of us, those comfort watches simply have to be Christmas rom-coms (perhaps with a bit of Home Alone thrown in). There’s an unrivaled comfort to a love story that plays out to a stripped-back piano version of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,” some fake snow, and a will-they-won’t-they New Year’s countdown. Maybe it’s the champs talking, but you truly can’t beat it.

To that end, here are some of the best Christmas rom-coms of all time.

Based on the newspaper column and subsequent book by Helen Fielding, the story is told through diary entries by the titular Bridget Jones, played by Renée Zellweger (as you probably well know). Of course, Bridget is the blueprint for the frazzled Englishwoman trope—with her laddered tights, cooking mishaps, and pretty much always saying and doing slightly the wrong thing—but who could fail to fall for her? Certainly not Daniel Cleaver (Hugh Grant) or Mark Darcy (Colin Firth), whose rivalry culminates in one of the greatest slapstick brawls in cinematic history. So genuinely funny, heartwarming, and perfectly cast, we can even begrudgingly overlook the problematic fact that Bridget’s weight was a subplot of its own.

Starring Will Ferrell as an enormous yet child-like elf who was born human but grew up in the North Pole with Santa and his crew, this John Favreau-directed film became an instant classic upon release in 2003. With anyone else but Ferrell in the lead, this movie could have flopped, but he plays Buddy to perfection. (Hands up if you still quote, “Daddy, Daddy, I’m in love and I don’t care who knows it!”) Buddy travels to New York to find his real father, played by James Caan, who turns out to be a grump who has absolutely zero festive cheer. Luckily, his son is an elf who can help him discover the true meaning of Christmas—and turn his failing children’s book company around in the process. The rom part of this rom-com is courtesy of Zooey Deschanel, who plays the department store worker who falls for Buddy.

Christmas doesn’t officially start until you’ve done your annual rewatch of Richard Curtis’s Love, Actually (we don’t make the rules!). The ultimate ensemble movie, with its various subplots culminates in a grande finale involving a school nativity play, this film is like seven little films in one. There’s Martine McCutcheon as Downing Street staffer Natalie; Hugh Grant as the prime minister we’d all like in real life; Colin Firth as the stern, broken-hearted one who flees to France; Liam Neeson as the widower; Keira Knightley and Chiwetel Ejiofor as the newlyweds and Andrew Lincoln as their borderline-creepy best pal; Bill Nighy as a washed-up rocker; and Laura Linney nabbing the hottest office co-worker to ever live. Emma Thompson, meanwhile, delivers one of the most devastating scenes you’ll ever see (Joni Mitchell CDs were never the same again). Also featured: an ideal soundtrack (Dido, Gabrielle, Texas) that your mom would have cleaned to in the Noughties.

A highly-strung New Yorker, Meredith Morton, played by Sarah Jessica Parker, goes to Connecticut to meet her boyfriend Everett Stone’s bohemian, eccentric, and extremely close-knit family at their home for the holidays. Everett (Dermot Mulroney) plans to propose with a family heirloom (ahh! The family stone!), but after a rocky start, his family is going to need some persuading that Meredith is right for him…and them. It’s not your straightforward warm and fuzzy movie, but it’s far more unique than anything made today, and the cast really is stellar (the late Diane Keaton, Claire Danes, Rachel McAdams, and Luke Wilson all appear). One to rewatch before the sequel, The Families Stone (yes, really), drops in November 2027.

Nancy Meyers outdid herself with this one. The set-up is simple: Amanda (Cameron Diaz) and Iris (Kate Winslet) are suffering the most dreadful romantic woes thanks to the men in their lives, played by Edward Burns and Rufus Sewell. And so they find themselves on an early sort of Airbnb to initiate a house swap, with Amanda staying in Iris’s chocolate box Cotswolds home while Iris jets to Amanda’s Los Angeles mansion. They are on a mission to “find themselves” and, by golly, that involves some snogging. Iris falls for musician Miles, played by Jack Black, Amanda gets Graham, a widowed father-of-two played by Jude Law. It’s all so lovely, there’s rarely been a film more capable of calming one’s nervous system.

Not to be confused with Nancy Meyers’s bicontinental confection—nor with 2019’s Last Christmas, starring Emilia Clarke and Henry Golding and co-written by Emma Thompson—Last Holiday, directed by Wayne Wang (Joy Luck Club, Maid in Manhattan), is loosely based on a 1950 British film of the same name. This version stars Queen Latifah as Georgia Byrd, a selfless saleswoman from New Orleans who, upon learning she is terminally ill, books a lavish Christmastime visit to the Grandhotel Pupp in the Czech Republic, where she intends to squeeze every last indulgent moment out of the weeks she has left. If all that sounds a bit maudlin, trust that Queen Latifah makes an incredibly winning (and glamorous) leading lady, Timothy Hutton is delectable as a big-business villain, and LL Cool J is the love interest (!). (Yes, Gérard Depardieu is in there too, but don’t let him scare you off!)

I long for the weird days when Vince Vaughan starred in rom-coms. Sure, he’s a sort of unlikely leading man, but his ability to gruffly subvert a genre? No one does it like Vaughan. Four Christmases sees him star opposite fellow rom-com royalty Reese Witherspoon; they play Brad and Kate, a couple who avoid Christmas with their divorced parents each year by claiming to do charity work abroad (when they’re really going on a tropical holiday). One year, their flights get canceled because of widespread fog, their lie is outed by a news reporter on live TV, and they find themselves having to visit all four parents in a single day for four different Christmas celebrations.

#6638. This $20 Gadget Is My Grandpa’s Secret To Making Big-Batch Potatoes For The Holidays

It looks a little ridiculous, but I can’t stop watching it work.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

If you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

Mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up new recipes.

Since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

#6635. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6634. McQueen Pre-Fall 2027

During the interregnum between the departure of Seán McGirr and the arrival of his as-yet-unnamed successor, McQueen is taking a look at itself. For this pre-fall collection, the studio team used its take on the house codes as a mirror, focusing upon each member’s individual specialisms while ensuring the whole ensemble remained coherently connected.

In both womenswear and menswear, the objective was sophistication stimulated by visceral twists and visual misdirection. The at-first-glance glossy croc leather of pants worn under a sky-blue jacket in womenswear, and as a matching black set in menswear, was denim treated with a raised pigment print. An asymmetric lapel and lighter internal construction relaxed the formality of a gray checked men’s suit worn over a frogged shirt. There was an echo of British countrywear in a subtly snake-patterned brown wool jacquard women’s suit whose integrated leather-strapped harness cinched just below the bust. A trailing-wrap, flat-fronted Prince of Wales check kilt, pleated behind, was rendered in an unexpectedly light fabrication. The full-skirted strapless dress that closed the lookbook was fashioned from a specially developed black lace lacquered to create a sheeny surface flash. Golden viscose suiting shimmered.

In knitwear, the tangled skeins of spider lace—derived from Alexander McQueen’s 1994 Banshee collection—were reinterpreted in a fine openwork jacquard of cotton backed with silk. A closely fitted dress in shades of metallic jacquard was based on a laser-cut lace piece from the house’s spring 2012 collection and featured a grille of serrated-edged rib cage cutouts on the back.

The corsetry that informed some ready-to-wear was also reflected in the finely drawn lacing applied to boots and pumps. Sharply chiseled men’s formal shoes featured gently tarnished and spackled metal hardware. On some women’s pumps, additional spathes of almost patently glossy leather, worked with metal threads to allow their shape to be manipulated, were designed to resemble calla lilies. These also featured in embroidery or print; in pink against a graduated red ground on skirts and shirting, on the sleeves of a biker jacket, and through the blinds of a fitted dress in whose harness structure was slung with strips of sliced leather.

#6632. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested—and retested—just about every meal delivery service. Each time we try HelloFresh, we’re impressed by its bold flavors, so we teamed up with the brand to bring you our favorite recipes each week (read more about how we chose them here). Sign up for a delivery, and you also get a 3-month digital subscription to BA for free. Here’s a closer look at one of our BA Picks.

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

True to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

#6629. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, says of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman says. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

#6625. Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

While the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

Make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

When the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

#6624. 12 Best Hair Clippers in 2026: Tested by GQ Editors

There's no shame in the DIY hair-cutting game, and the best hair clippers will serve you well, whether you're trying to cut corners and save cash on those barbershop visits (parents, I see you!) or don’t need anything fancy beyond a half-inch DIY buzz cut. No matter how frequently you reach for them, the best hair clippers get the job done for you. But before I get into our picks, if you're looking for clipper inspiration, check out our at-home buzz cut guide, the best celebrity buzz cuts, as well as the imperative beard-to-hair ratio rules—so that you feel confident when it's time to take things into your own hand. Our top pick makes it easy to give yourself a straightforward home haircut – it gives the best DIY results, and costs much less than its competition. When it comes to at-home haircuts, I urge you to keep things simple. You do not need a lot of complexity from a device. Its color-coded guard system helps you gauge how much you're taking off and what you'll wind up with.

Between its 1/16” light green clip and the light blue, one-inch clip, the device has a terrific range of length options, with especially sturdy guards that do not have any “give,” meaning you always get consistent results.

This newest model has a lithium-ion battery that give it a long battery life—twice as long, in fact, as the previous option (two hours versus one) and will keep its juice for nine months idly without draining. This cordless trimmer is imperative to own for any parents who want to buzz their kids’ hair and save a fortune on frequent haircuts—especially since the kids can opt into so many different hair-cutting lengths and since it’s much easier to remember the length you used based on the color-coded system here. Normally, when you want to adjust a zero-gap clipper, you have to pop off the blade and manually adjust it with a tiny dial.
